targets.authors: Newman, D. A., Joseph, D. L., & Hulin, C. L.
targets.title: Job attitudes and employee engagement: Considering the "A-factor".
targets.evidence_quote: For the relationships among work engagement, job satisfaction, affective organizational commitment, and job involvement, we used the meta-analytic correlations from Newman et al. (2010). This allowed us to replicate and extend the work of Newman et al. by conducting new analyses on the same data.
targets.outcome_computational_quote: For example, our model produced estimated latent correlations from the A-factor of job attitudes to work engagement (φ=0.77), job satisfaction (φ=0.71), affective organizational commitment (φ=0.75), and job involvement (φ=0.72) that were identical to those reported by Newman et al. (2010). Only the RMSEA values differed slightly where our analysis yielded a value 0.006 lower than the value of 0.180 reported by Newman.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: Therefore, interpretation of relationships between factors such as those made by Newman et al. (2010) –and others –require analyses similar to those reported in the present study.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Original meta-analytic data reanalysed with variance decomposition, challenging redundancy interpretation. Original 2010 numerical model explicitly recovered up to minor fit-index variation; numerical reproduction of 2011 is not separately established. Both publications are directly re-examined; 2010 supplied the data and original numerical model, while 2011 states the challenged claim. Partial full-text extraction limits certainty, especially the scope of the 2010 robustness verdict.

targets.authors: Newman, D. A., Joseph, D. L., Sparkman, T. E., & Carpenter, N. C.
targets.title: Invited reaction: The work cognition inventory: Initial evidence of construct validity.
targets.evidence_quote: First, using the same data that Newman et al. (2011) reported, we retested the claim that the UWES yielded data appearing to be tapped into variance uniquely common to job satisfaction, affective organizational commitment, and job involvement.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: The variance that was uniquely common to job involvement, job satisfaction, and affective organizational commitment was 16.6% (see Table 3). With only 28% of the explained variance accounted for (0.166/0.588), this finding debunks the claim suggested by Newman et al. (2011) that UWES yields data that appear to be redundant with the variance that is uniquely common to job satisfaction, affective organizational commitment, and job involvement.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Original meta-analytic data reanalysed with variance decomposition, challenging redundancy interpretation. Original 2010 numerical model explicitly recovered up to minor fit-index variation; numerical reproduction of 2011 is not separately established. Both publications are directly re-examined; 2010 supplied the data and original numerical model, while 2011 states the challenged claim. Partial full-text extraction limits certainty, especially the scope of the 2010 robustness verdict.
